speaker: NARRATOR
text: In 2012, researchers looked at data on nearly thirty thousand American adults. They'd been asked two simple questions.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: How much stress do you have?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And do you believe stress is hurting your health?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Then the researchers waited, and looked at who had died over the following years.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The people with a lot of stress, who believed it was harming them... had a 43 percent higher risk of dying early.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [warmer, leaning in] But here's what nobody expected. People with just as much stress... who didn't see it as harmful... didn't show that risk at all. In fact, they had some of the lowest risk in the whole study.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: [slow] Same pressure. Different story. Different outcome.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It's one study. It can't prove the belief itself caused it. But it raises a question worth sitting with.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: What if part of what hurts us... is the way we were taught to see it?
